category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: For the prevention of percutaneous injuries, used needles and scalpel blades must be placed immediately into a puncture-resistant [___] at the point of use.
back:
• Sharps container (or Safety Box)
• Must be leak-proof and rigid
• Filled only to the marked 3/4 line
• Located within arm's reach of the procedure

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A house officer sustains a needle-stick injury while attempting to recap a syringe manually after a blood draw. Identify the procedural violation and the immediate safety requirement for the used needle.
back:
• Manual recapping is strictly prohibited
• Use 'single-handed scoop' if necessary
• Immediate disposal into sharps bin
• Report as occupational exposure incident

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Explain the biological and safety rationale behind the 'no-touch technique' when managing contaminated clinical waste.
back:
• Prevents direct contact with pathogens
• Reduces risk of accidental inoculation
• Minimizes cross-contamination of surfaces
• Employs forceps or tools for handling sharps

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Contrast the disposal requirements for blood-soaked laparotomy sponges with those for used surgical staples.
back:
• Sponges: Leak-proof biohazard bags (Yellow)
• Staples: Rigid sharps containers
• Sponges require incineration/autoclaving
• Staples require puncture-resistant containment

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Detail the protocol for disposing of a vaccine vial that has lost its label or shows signs of contamination in a clinical setting.
back:
• Immediate withdrawal from clinical use
• Disposal in designated infectious waste bin
• Management according to cold-chain/waste protocols
• Notification of the local health authority

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: In resource-poor environments, the reuse of syringes or needles without [___] is a major driver of iatrogenic transmission of HIV and Hepatitis viruses.
back:
• Proper sterilization
• Prevents approx. 1.3 million deaths annually
• Breaks the chain of transmission
• Mandates 'one needle, one syringe, one time'

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A surgical team is managing a case involving a patient with a known bloodborne pathogen. Describe the specific modifications required for handling sharps on the instrument trolley.
back:
• Use of a 'neutral zone' for passing
• Elimination of hand-to-hand passing
• Immediate disposal by the user
• Utilization of blunt-tip needles when feasible

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Describe the mechanism by which the 'safety box' prevents the spread of infection in community-based immunization programs.
back:
• Provides a physical barrier to injuries
• Prevents scavenging of used equipment
• Facilitates safe transport to incineration sites
• Ensures containment of residual fluids

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Contrast the final disposal pathway of 'Infectious Clinical Waste' (Yellow bag) with 'General Hospital Waste' (Black/Blue bag).
back:
• Infectious: Incineration or deep burial
• General: Municipal waste management/landfill
• Infectious requires sterilization/neutralization
• General must not contain sharps/liquids

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Identify the primary mandatory physical characteristics of a sharps container intended for surgical ward use.
back:
• Puncture-proof material (e.g., heavy plastic)
• Leak-proof bottom and sides
• Secured, tamper-proof lid
• Clear biohazard labeling/color coding

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: To prevent percutaneous injuries in clinical settings, used needles and scalpels must be discarded immediately into a dedicated, [___] container at the point of use.
back: Puncture-resistant sharps container. Key safety points include: • Never recapping used needles. • Disposing of sharps at the source. • Ensuring containers are never overfilled beyond the three-quarters mark.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A medical student accidentally pricks their finger while attempting to recap a needle after a blood draw. Identify the immediate first-aid step and the standard precaution rule that was violated.
back: The site should be washed immediately with soap and water. The student violated the 'no-recapping' rule, which mandates that used needles must be discarded without manipulation into a sharps box.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Explain the protocol for the safe handling and disposal of linen heavily soiled with patient secretions in a healthcare setting where mechanical washing facilities are unavailable.
back: Soiled linen should be boiled to ensure effective disinfection. This process utilizes high temperature to kill vegetative pathogens before final disposal or reuse, protecting laundry staff from infectious exposure.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Contrast the disposal requirements for a blood-soaked surgical dressing versus a clean paper towel used for hand drying in the wards.
back: • Blood-soaked dressing: Classified as infectious waste; disposed in yellow biohazard bags for incineration. • Paper towel: Classified as general/municipal waste; disposed in standard black bins.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Identify the core principle of the 'no-touch technique' during the handling and disposal of contaminated surgical instruments.
back: It involves using mechanical instruments like forceps, rather than fingers, to handle sharps or contaminated items. This minimizes direct hand contact and prevents accidental percutaneous injuries and cross-contamination.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: In the hospital waste stream, heat-sensitive surgical plastics and delicate instruments that cannot undergo autoclaving are typically sterilized using [___] gas.
back: Ethylene oxide. It acts as an alkylating agent to kill microorganisms and spores at lower temperatures, making it ideal for materials that would melt or corrode in steam.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A nurse is tasked with disposing of 500ml of purulent pleural fluid after a drainage procedure. Describe the high-yield safety steps for managing this liquid infectious waste.
back: The fluid should be disinfected (e.g., with 1% hypochlorite) before disposal into a clinical drain. Personnel must use PPE, including gloves and face shields, to prevent splash injuries.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Describe the mechanism by which the 'Standard Precautions' framework integrates waste management into routine patient care.
back: It treats all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious. It mandates immediate sharps disposal at the bedside and the use of PPE when handling any waste contaminated with biological fluids.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Distinguish between the waste items intended for a yellow puncture-resistant bin versus those intended for a yellow biohazard plastic bag.
back: • Yellow Bin: Strictly for sharps (needles, scalpels, broken glass). • Yellow Bag: For non-sharp infectious waste (gloves, swabs, blood-contaminated gauze, and pathological waste).

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Specify the required action for managing used multi-dose vaccine vials that have lost their labels or show signs of moisture contamination.
back: These vials must be discarded immediately as infectious waste. Using unlabelled or potentially contaminated vials is a major cause of iatrogenic infections and Programmatic Errors in immunization.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: To prevent accidental percutaneous injury, healthcare workers must strictly avoid the practice of [___] needles after clinical use.
back:
• Recapping (sheathing)
• This practice is a major cause of needle-stick injuries
• Needles should be disposed of immediately into sharps containers

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A nurse finishes an injection and is looking for a place to discard the syringe. According to standard precautions, the needle must be discarded immediately into a [___] container.
back:
• Puncture-resistant sharps box
• Must be leak-proof and clearly labeled
• Located as close as possible to the point of use

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Explain the role of 'puncture-resistance' in the design of sharps disposal systems for hospital-acquired infection (HAI) control.
back:
• Prevents needles from protruding through walls
• Protects waste handlers from percutaneous exposure
• Essential for safe transport and final disposal

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A ward manager is organizing waste protocols. Contrast the disposal pathway for general administrative paper with that of gauze heavily soaked in a patient's peritoneal fluid.
back:
• General waste: Black bags for municipal disposal
• Clinical waste: Yellow/biohazard bags for incineration
• Clinical waste requires specialized handling to prevent environmental contamination

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Identify the recommended alternative for disinfecting hospital linen contaminated with infective material when a dedicated mechanical washing machine is unavailable.
back:
• Boiling the linen
• Effective for thermal disinfection of common pathogens
• Should be done before standard laundering if contamination is high

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: In resource-limited settings where needles or syringes are reused, safety depends entirely on rigorous [___] before the next patient encounter.
back:
• Sterilization (e.g., autoclaving)
• Prevents transmission of blood-borne viruses
• Boiling is often insufficient for complete sterilization of spores

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: An intern notices a blood spill on the floor after a central line insertion. According to standard precautions, identify the immediate necessary action.
back:
• Promptly clean up the spill
• Use appropriate chemical disinfectants (e.g., hypochlorite)
• Wear PPE (gloves/gown) during the cleaning process

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Describe the mechanism by which the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist 'Sign-Out' phase prevents the occurrence of retained sharps within a patient.
back:
• Mandatory verbal confirmation of instrument counts
• Accounting for all needles and swabs used
• Prevents 'Never Events' and subsequent post-operative infections

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Contrast the handling of reusable patient-care equipment (like a pulse oximeter) with single-use items (like a disposable syringe) following contact with a patient in isolation.
back:
• Reusable: Disinfected or sterilized between patients
• Single-use: Discarded as clinical waste immediately
• Prevents cross-contamination via the hospital environment

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Beyond needle-stick injuries, identify the primary blood-borne pathogens transmitted globally due to the reuse of unsterilized syringes.
back:
• Hepatitis B virus (HBV)
• Hepatitis C virus (HCV)
• Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)
• Causes approximately 1.3 million deaths annually

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: In clinical settings, used needles and scalpels must be immediately discarded into a puncture-resistant, leak-proof container known as a [___].
back:
* Sharps container (Sharp box)
* Typically color-coded (Yellow)
* Must be puncture-resistant to prevent percutaneous injury
* Placed at the point of use for immediate disposal.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A house officer accidentally pricks their finger while suturing a patient with unknown serology. Identify the immediate first step in the management of this injury.
back:
* Wash the site thoroughly with soap and water
* Avoid scrubbing or squeezing the wound
* Report to the Infection Control Department
* Evaluate for HBV, HCV, and HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP).

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Explain the safety rationale for mandating the 'one-handed scoop' technique if recapping a needle is absolutely necessary.
back:
* Prevents accidental needle-stick injury to the opposing hand
* Minimizes the risk of blood-borne pathogen transmission (HBV, HCV, HIV)
* Standardizes handling of contaminated needles until they reach the sharps box.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Contrast the disposal requirements for a blood-soaked dressing versus a used glass medication ampoule in a surgical ward.
back:
* Blood-soaked dressing: Yellow biohazard bag (infectious waste)
* Glass ampoule: Puncture-resistant sharps container
* Sharps containers prevent physical injury to waste handlers from broken glass or metal.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: List the three primary blood-borne pathogens that pose the highest risk to healthcare workers during improper sharps disposal.
back:
* Hepatitis B Virus (HBV)
* Hepatitis C Virus (HCV)
* Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)
* These require strict adherence to standard precautions and safe disposal.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: To prevent overflow and accidental injury, sharps containers must be sealed and sent for disposal once they reach [___] of their total capacity.
back:
* Three-quarters (3/4) full
* Never overfill or force needles into a full container
* Prevents accidental protrusion of needles through the lid.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A nurse is observed leaving used syringes on a bedside tray to dispose of them after the morning round. Explain the hazard created by this delay.
back:
* Creates 'Coal-face' error risk for other staff or patients
* Increases the likelihood of accidental needle-sticks during bed-making or cleaning
* Violates the 'dispose at source' safety protocol.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Describe the physiological objective of utilizing high-temperature incineration for the final disposal of sharps waste.
back:
* Ensures total sterilization of microbial load
* Renders the physical sharp (metal/glass) non-recognizable and non-reusable
* Reduces the volume of biohazardous waste before landfilling.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Distinguish between the disposal color-coding for infectious medical waste and non-infectious general waste in a hospital.
back:
* Infectious Waste: Yellow bag/bin (e.g., dressings, tissue)
* General Waste: Black bag/bin (e.g., paper, food wrappers)
* Proper segregation reduces the cost and environmental impact of incineration.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Identify the safest instrument-assisted method for removing a used blade from a scalpel handle.
back:
* Use a needle holder or forceps to grip the blade
* Point the blade away from the body during removal
* Immediately drop the blade into a yellow sharps container.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: To prevent percutaneous injuries in the ward, all used needles and scalpel blades must be immediately discarded into a yellow-coded, [___] container.
back:
● Puncture-resistant (or puncture-proof).
● Prevents accidental needle-stick injuries.
● Located at the point of use.
● Prevents needle protrusion during transport.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A house officer sustains a needle-stick injury while disposing of a syringe used on a Hepatitis B positive patient. Specify the mandatory immediate first step.
back:
● Wash the wound with soap and water.
● Do not squeeze or scrub the site.
● Report immediately for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).
● Check baseline serology for HBV, HCV, and HIV.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Explain the segregation criteria for clinical waste placed in yellow bags versus red bags in a surgical unit.
back:
● Yellow Bags: Infectious/pathological waste and dressings.
● Red Bags: Contaminated plastic waste like IV sets and catheters.
● Segregation prevents cross-contamination and optimizes final disposal methods (Incineration vs Autoclaving).

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Contrast the safety risks of the traditional two-handed recapping method with the recommended 'one-handed scoop' technique for needle disposal.
back:
● Two-handed: High risk of accidental finger puncture due to proximity.
● One-handed scoop: Needle remains stationary on a flat surface; cap is guided on without manual handling.
● Scoop is only used if immediate disposal is unavailable.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Identify the primary mechanical intervention used at the bedside to render needles unusable and non-reusable immediately after a procedure.
back:
● Needle destroyers or hub cutters.
● Electrically burns the needle or mechanically shears the hub.
● Prevents illicit reuse of discarded syringes.
● Reduces the volume of sharp waste.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: To maintain safety standards and prevent protruding sharp hazards, sharps containers must be sealed and replaced once they reach [___] of their total capacity.
back:
● Three-quarters (3/4 or 75%).
● Prevents overfilling and spillages.
● Ensures the lid can be securely locked.
● Minimizes exposure during final waste collection.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Following an appendectomy, the surgical team needs to dispose of the excised appendix. Determine the correct waste stream and the standard final disposal method.
back:
● Waste Stream: Yellow bag (Infectious/Anatomical waste).
● Final Method: High-temperature incineration.
● Prevents environmental pathogen spread.
● Ensures complete destruction of biological hazards.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Explain the biological safety mechanism provided by high-temperature incineration compared to deep burial for hazardous medical waste.
back:
● Incineration: Thermal destruction of pathogens and volume reduction.
● Deep Burial: Physical isolation in lined pits.
● Incineration is preferred for highly infectious and anatomical waste to ensure total sterility.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Contrast the use of 1% Sodium Hypochlorite with autoclaving for the decontamination of infectious liquid laboratory waste.
back:
● 1% Sodium Hypochlorite: Chemical disinfection for blood spills/liquids.
● Autoclaving: Thermal sterilization via pressurized steam.
● Both processes neutralize pathogens before final discharge into the hospital sewerage system.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: List the essential personal protective equipment (PPE) required for hospital staff when transporting bio-medical waste to the central storage area.
back:
● Heavy-duty utility gloves.
● Puncture-resistant rubber boots.
● Plastic apron or protective gown.
● Face shield or mask if splashing is anticipated.

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: The primary physical method for achieving sterilization of medical glassware and heat-stable surgical instruments requires exposure to steam in an autoclave at [___]°C for at least 15 minutes.
back:
- 121°C.
- Performed at 15 lb/in² pressure.
- Parameters are specifically designed to kill highly heat-resistant bacterial spores.

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: A 60-year-old female presents with pyrexia and flank pain 10 years after an abdominal hysterectomy; imaging confirms a retained surgical swab. Classify this specific category of healthcare incident.
back:
- Never Event (Serious Reportable Event).
- Defined as a wholly preventable event where strong systemic protective barriers (e.g., WHO checklist) failed.
- Mandates open disclosure and root-cause analysis.

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which the presence of water (e.g., in a 70% concentration) improves the antimicrobial efficacy of ethanol during skin disinfection.
back:
- Water facilitates protein denaturation by disrupting non-covalent (hydrogen) bonds.
- Prevents rapid evaporation, increasing the contact time with microbial membranes.
- Aids in the disorganization of the lipid membrane structure.

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: A surgical nurse is preparing for a list. Contrast the protective measures required for 'Contact Precautions' in a MRSA case with those required for 'High Security' isolation in a suspected viral hemorrhagic fever case.
back:
- Contact: Basic gown and gloves to prevent surface transfer.
- High Security (e.g., Ebola): Full body protection, including masks, eye protection, and double gloving to prevent any mucosal/skin contact with blood or body fluids.

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Identify the specific pharmacological agent and its biochemical mechanism of action preferred for skin preparation prior to obtaining blood cultures to minimize contamination risk.
back:
- Tincture of Iodine (2% iodine/potassium iodide in ethanol).
- Mechanism: Acts as an oxidant that inactivates sulfhydryl-containing enzymes and binds specifically to tyrosine residues in microbial proteins.

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: According to the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist protocols, the 'Sign In' phase must be verbally completed with the nurse and anaesthetist before [___].
back:
- Induction of anaesthesia.
- Key checks: Patient identity, site marking, procedure consent, and pulse oximeter function.

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: A surgical team realizes an incision is being planned on the wrong limb during the 'Time Out' phase and corrects it before the cut is made. Classify this event and its clinical significance.
back:
- Near-miss event.
- Significance: Highlights a breakdown in safety layers (Swiss Cheese Model) that was caught by chance or intervention before actual harm reached the patient.

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Describe the biochemical mechanism by which ethylene oxide gas achieves sterilization of heat-sensitive items like surgical plastics and sutures.
back:
- Acts as an alkylating agent.
- Adds a hydroxyethyl group to reactive hydrogen atoms on essential amino and hydroxyl groups.
- Permanently modifies/inactivates microbial proteins and nucleic acids.

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Contrast the physiological factors that allow 'Aerotolerant' organisms to survive in air versus 'Obligate Anaerobes' which are killed by oxygen exposure.
back:
- Aerotolerant (e.g., C. histolyticum): Possess minimal adaptive enzymes to survive oxygen but do not use it for growth.
- Obligate Anaerobes (e.g., B. fragilis): Lack catalase and superoxide dismutase (SOD), leading to lethal accumulation of hydrogen peroxide and superoxide.

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
coreConcept: WHO Five Moments for Hand Hygiene
front: Name the five specific moments for hand hygiene defined by the WHO to reduce infection transmission in healthcare settings.
back:
1. Before touching a patient.
2. Before a clean/aseptic procedure.
3. After body fluid exposure risk.
4. After touching a patient.
5. After touching patient surroundings.

• Prev ents percutan eous injury
• Ensures pat hogen destru ction

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Describe the role of Ethylene Oxide gas in the hospital waste management and sterilization cycle.
back:
• Sterilizati on of heat-se nsitive mate rials
• Alkyla tes proteins  and nucleic  acids
• Used  for plastics  and optical  scopes
• Req uires aerati on for resid ue removal

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Distinguish between sterilization and disinfection in the context of hospital waste management.
back:
• Sterilizati on: Total mic robial death  incl. spores
• Disinfectio n: Kills pat hogens, but  not all spor es
• Sterili zation uses  autoclaves/ga s
• Disinfec tion uses ch emicals (e.g . alcohols)

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Identify the clinical disposal protocol for anatomical waste, such as a gallbladder removed during cholecystectomy.
back:
• Yellow/Red  leak-proof b iohazard bag s
• Labeled  as 'Anatomic al Waste'
• De stined for i ncineration  or deep buri al
• Prevents  environmen tal contami nation

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: To minimize percutaneous injuries, sharps must be discarded into a leak-proof, puncture-resistant container prominently labeled with the [___] symbol.
back:
● Biohazard symbol
● Ensures clear identification of infectious hazards
● Required by standard precautions for all clinical settings.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A nurse finishes an injection and prepares to recap the needle before disposal. To prevent accidental injury, the recommended method if recapping is absolutely necessary is [___].
back:
● One-hand 'scoop' technique
● Avoids using both hands near the needle point
● Significantly reduces risk of needlestick injuries.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Explain the role of 'Point of Use' disposal in the management of surgical sharps.
back:
● Immediate disposal at the site of use
● Prevents transport of exposed needles
● Minimizes risk to downstream housekeeping staff.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Contrast the disposal requirements for a discarded glass vaccine vial versus a blood-contaminated disposable gown.
back:
● Glass Vials: Sharps container (yellow bin with hard walls)
● Gowns: Yellow biohazard bag (soft-walled bin)
● Prevents puncture of plastic bags by glass.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Identify the critical fill-level threshold at which a sharps container must be sealed and replaced to prevent over-spilling.
back:
● Three-quarters (3/4) full
● Prevents needles from protruding from the top
● Ensures safe closure and transport.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: In the hospital waste management hierarchy, non-infectious general waste like paper or fruit peels is segregated into [___] colored bags.
back:
● Black bags
● Dedicated for domestic/municipal waste
● Reduces the cost and volume of incineration.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A surgical team completes a laparotomy. During the final count, the primary protocol for disposing of used scalpel blades and curved suture needles is [___].
back:
● Placement in a rigid sharps box
● Never discarded in standard trash or soft bags
● Counted against the pre-op tally to ensure no retained items.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Describe the physiological objective of using high-temperature incineration for pathological waste like excised tissue.
back:
● Complete sterilization of pathogens
● Reduction of mass and volume
● Ensures biological materials are unrecognizable and inert.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Contrast the treatment of liquid infectious waste (e.g., blood or suctioned fluids) with solid infectious waste.
back:
● Liquid: Chemical disinfection (bleach) or sealed drainage
● Solid: Autoclaving or yellow-bag incineration
● Prevents aerosolization of pathogens.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Name the primary device used at the ward level to immediately render needles non-functional and safe for container disposal.
back:
● Needle destroyer or cutter
● Mechanically shears or melts the needle
● Prevents illicit reuse of syringes.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: To prevent the healthcare-associated transmission of bloodborne viruses like HIV and Hepatitis B, all used needles and blades must be discarded at the point of use into a rigid, leak-proof, and [___].
back: Puncture-resistant sharps container (or Sharps Box).

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: A junior resident is observed manually recapping a used needle after performing a venipuncture on an ICU patient. Identify the specific safety violation and the recommended safe handling procedure for this device.
back:
Violation: Recapping used needles (major risk for percutaneous injury).
Procedure: Immediate disposal without recapping or manipulation into a designated sharps container.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Explain the mechanical rationale for segregating clinical waste into flexible biohazard bags (Yellow/Red) versus rigid sharps containers.
back:
- Biohazard Bags: Designed for soft waste (e.g., blood-soaked gauze) to provide a leak-proof barrier against fluids.
- Rigid Containers: Designed to provide a mechanical barrier that prevents percutaneous injury from sharp metal objects.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: The technique used to handle sterile equipment without direct hand contact, thereby minimizing the risk of contamination during invasive clinical procedures, is known as the [___] technique.
back:
*   Known as the "No-touch" technique.
*   Involves using sterile forceps or gloves.
*   Prevents direct transfer of pathogens from clinician hands to sterile sites or devices.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A 25-year-old male is prepared for venipuncture using 70% ethanol. Explain the specific biochemical mechanism by which this agent inactivates microorganisms.
back:
*   Disorganizes the lipid structure in cell membranes.
*   Causes denaturation of cellular proteins.
*   Requires water for maximal activity (hence 70% is superior to 100%).

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain how the maintenance of a strictly closed drainage system prevents the development of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections (CAUTI).
back:
*   Acts as a physical barrier to ascending intraluminal migration.
*   Prevents environmental organisms from entering the urinary tract.
*   Minimizes frequency of disconnection, a major risk factor for contamination.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Contrast the aseptic requirements for the insertion of a peripheral venous cannula with those required for a central venous catheter (CVC).
back:
*   Peripheral: Requires standard aseptic technique (clean gloves, localized skin antisepsis).
*   Central (CVC): Requires full surgical asepsis (sterile gown, mask, cap, and large sterile drapes).

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the specific clinical indication for using iodine-containing compounds (Iodophors) rather than simple 70% alcohol for skin preparation.
back:
*   Prior to obtaining blood cultures.
*   Prior to installing central intravenous catheters.
*   Used because iodine is more effective at eliminating persistent skin flora like S. epidermidis.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: In surgical site infection (SSI) surveillance, a primary infection is categorized as an SSI if purulent discharge or abscess formation occurs within [___] after the operative procedure.
back:
*   One month (30 days).
*   The criteria applies to discharge from the incision or deep tissues.
*   Essential for standardized hospital-acquired infection reporting.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: An ICU patient is mechanically ventilated. To reduce the risk of Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP), the nursing team focuses on aseptic suctioning and [___].
back:
*   Limiting the duration of intubation.
*   Using non-invasive ventilation modes when possible.
*   Aseptic intubation techniques and regular oral care with chlorhexidine.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain why 70% ethanol is clinically more effective as an antiseptic compared to 100% absolute ethanol.
back:
*   Ethanol requires water for its maximal antimicrobial activity.
*   Water facilitates the denaturation of proteins.
*   Water aids in the penetration of the bacterial cell wall.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Distinguish between the terms 'Disinfectant' and 'Antiseptic' based on their target application surfaces.
back:
*   Disinfectants: Chemicals used on inanimate objects (e.g., floors, surgical equipment).
*   Antiseptics: Milder chemicals safe for use on living skin or mucous membranes.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the preoperative skin preparation practice that is now proven to be ineffective and potentially harmful in preventing surgical site infections.
back:
*   Preoperative shaving (especially with razors).
*   Creates micro-abrasions that harbor bacteria.
*   Alternative: Use of electric clippers only if hair interferes with the procedure.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Sterilization of surgical instruments via autoclaving is achieved by exposure to steam at a temperature of [___] under 15 lb/in² of pressure for 15 minutes.
back:
* 121°C
* Kills all microorganisms including highly resistant bacterial spores
* Standard method for moisture/heat-tolerant equipment.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A surgeon is preparing to insert a central venous catheter. To prevent contamination by skin flora like Staphylococcus epidermidis, the most effective antiseptic for site preparation is [___].
back:
* Iodine-containing compounds (e.g., Iodophors or Tincture of Iodine)
* Superior to alcohol alone for deep invasive procedures
* Requires drying time for maximum efficacy.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism of action of 70% Ethanol as an antiseptic and why it is not used as a 100% solution.
back:
* Denatures proteins and disorganizes lipid structures in cell membranes
* Requires water for maximal activity (hence 70% vs 100%)
* Rapidly bactericidal but does not kill spores.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Contrast the application of Glutaraldehyde with Ethylene oxide in the management of invasive medical devices.
back:
* Glutaraldehyde: Liquid chemical for endoscopes, respiratory, and hemodialysis equipment.
* Ethylene oxide: Gas sterilization for heat-sensitive plastics and surgical instruments.
* Both are effective against spores.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the preoperative practice involving hair removal that is proven 'not effective' at reducing surgical site infections (SSIs) and should be avoided.
back:
* Preoperative shaving (razors cause micro-abrasions)
* Clipping is preferred if hair removal is necessary
* Shaving increases risk of bacterial colonization.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: To ensure intravenous solutions are pyrogen-free and sterilized without heat, they are passed through filters with a pore size of [___].
back:
* 0.22 μm
* Retains all bacteria and spores
* Prevents fever caused by heat-resistant endotoxins from dead gram-negative bacteria.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A patient requires an indwelling urinary catheter. According to evidence-based infection prevention protocols, which measure is most critical to prevent CAUTI?
back:
* Limiting the duration of catheterization
* Maintaining a strictly closed drainage system
* Using aseptic technique during insertion.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: How does Chlorine (hypochlorite) achieve microbial killing during the disinfection of hospital surfaces?
back:
* Acts as a powerful oxidizing agent
* Cross-links essential sulfhydryl groups in bacterial enzymes
* Forms inactive disulfides, disrupting metabolic function.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Distinguish between 'Antiseptics' and 'Disinfectants' regarding their clinical application sites.
back:
* Antiseptics: Applied to living tissue (skin/mucous membranes) to kill microbes.
* Disinfectants: Applied only to inanimate objects/surfaces (floors/equipment) due to toxicity/causticity.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the single most common and effective route to interrupt the chain of transmission for healthcare-associated infections.
back:
* Hand-washing/Hand hygiene
* Prevents direct contact transfer from staff to susceptible patients
* WHO "5 Moments" for hand hygiene is the gold standard.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: The standardized framework used in healthcare to prevent the transfer of microorganisms by ensuring 'Key Parts' and 'Key Sites' of invasive devices are not touched is known as [___].
back:
• Aseptic Non-Touch Technique (ANTT)
• Protects critical sites (e.g., IV hubs, wounds)
• Ensures only sterilized equipment contacts these areas
• Prevents accidental contamination during bedside procedures

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
coreConcept: Central Line Site Selection and Antisepsis
front: A surgeon is inserting a central venous catheter. To reduce the risk of healthcare-associated infection, the [___] vein is preferred over the femoral vein, and skin preparation must use [___].
back:
• Subclavian vein (lowest infection risk)
• >0.5% Chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% alcohol
• Provides rapid-acting and persistent antimicrobial activity
• Part of the 'Central Line Bundle'

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain the biological function of surgical asepsis (sterile technique) compared to medical asepsis (clean technique) in the handling of invasive devices.
back:
• Surgical Asepsis: Eliminates all microorganisms and spores; required for sterile body cavity entry
• Medical Asepsis: Reduces number and growth of pathogens; prevents cross-contamination
• Surgical uses sterile barriers; Medical uses clean gloves

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Contrast the infection prevention protocols for peripheral IV catheters versus central venous catheters regarding site inspection and replacement strategy.
back:
• Peripheral: Inspected daily for phlebitis; replaced if dysfunction occurs (routinely 72–96 hours)
• Central: Routine replacement not recommended solely for infection prevention
• Central requires sterile dressing changes with chlorhexidine; Peripheral uses clean technique

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Describe the specific handling protocol for an endotracheal tube and the oral cavity to prevent Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP).
back:
• Maintain cuff pressure (20–30 cm H2O) to prevent microaspiration
• Perform oral hygiene using chlorhexidine solution regularly
• Elevate head of bed to 30–45 degrees
• Suction subglottic secretions frequently

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Immediate-use steam sterilization (flash sterilization) of invasive surgical instruments is only permissible when [___].
back:
• An essential instrument is dropped or urgently needed
• Item is delivered immediately to the sterile field
• Never used for implanted devices (e.g., orthopedic hardware)
• Must follow rigorous cleaning before processing

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A nurse identifies a physical break in the junction between a patient's urinary catheter and the drainage bag. State the mandatory corrective action required.
back:
• Replace the entire catheter and drainage system immediately
• Maintain a sterile, continuously closed system
• Disconnection allows intraluminal entry of bacteria
• Standard action to prevent CAUTI

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain how the interaction between microorganisms and the polymer surface of an invasive device (e.g., a prosthetic heart valve) leads to persistent infection.
back:
• Microbes attach and secrete an extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix
• Form a 'biofilm' that protects bacteria from host immunity
• Biofilm hinders antibiotic penetration
• Usually requires device removal to achieve cure

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Differentiate the handling requirements for 'Critical' devices (e.g., cardiac catheters) versus 'Semi-critical' devices (e.g., endoscopes) according to Spaulding’s classification.
back:
• Critical: Enter sterile tissue or vascular system; require absolute sterilization
• Semi-critical: Contact mucous membranes/non-intact skin; require high-level disinfection
• Critical items pose the highest risk of infection transmission

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the standard high-yield timeframe for changing intravenous administration sets for non-lipid, non-blood continuous infusions.
back:
• Change tubing no more frequently than every 96 hours
• Interval can extend to 7 days with sterile access
• Lipid emulsions or blood products require change within 24 hours
• Minimizes bacterial colonization from frequent disconnections

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: For the sterilization of heat-sensitive invasive surgical instruments and plastics that cannot undergo high-temperature autoclaving, the primary chemical gas used is [___].
back:
* Ethylene Oxide (EtO).
* Acts by alkylating proteins and nucleic acids.
* Required for heat-labile materials like specialized catheters and optical scopes.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A patient in the ICU on mechanical ventilation is at risk for pneumonia. Identify the primary non-invasive management strategy to minimize the duration of endotracheal intubation and reduce the incidence of VAP.
back:
* Transition to non-invasive ventilation (NIV).
* Limits mechanical exposure to the lower respiratory tract.
* Reduces the entry of oropharyngeal flora via invasive tubes.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain the biological importance of maintaining a 'closed drainage system' in the safe handling of indwelling urinary catheters.
back:
* Prevents extraluminal bacterial entry.
* Minimizes contamination of the sterile collection bag.
* Interrupts the upward migration of pathogens into the bladder.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Contrast the aseptic requirements and technical approaches of 'endotracheal intubation' versus 'tracheal suctioning' in preventing respiratory tract infections.
back:
* Intubation: Requires strict sterile technique to prevent introducing oral flora during insertion.
* Suctioning: Uses Aseptic Non-Touch Technique (ANTT) with sterile catheters to clear secretions safely.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the essential safety protocols regarding the handling and disposal of 'sharps' following an invasive medical procedure.
back:
* Use 'no-touch' transfer techniques.
* Immediate disposal into puncture-resistant, labeled containers.
* Strict prohibition of recapping used needles.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: According to the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, the mandatory check performed immediately before the skin incision to confirm the team, site, and procedure is called the [___].
back:
* Time Out phase.
* Confirms patient identity and surgical site.
* Verifies antibiotic prophylaxis administration within the preceding 60 minutes.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A clinician is inserting a central venous catheter. Beyond standard sterile barriers, identify the preferred chemical protocol for skin preparation to reduce device-related bloodstream infections.
back:
* Use of chlorhexidine-based antiseptic (e.g., 2% in alcohol).
* Allow full air-drying for maximum efficacy.
* Avoid routine antimicrobial ointment application to the site.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Describe how the 'Aseptic Non-Touch Technique' (ANTT) carries out its biological function during the assembly and insertion of invasive devices.
back:
* Protects 'Key Parts' (e.g., needle hubs, catheter tips) from manual contact.
* Maintains a sterile field without requiring a full operating theater environment.
* Minimizes transfer of skin commensals to invasive components.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Contrast the impact of 'preoperative antiseptic showers' with 'hair shaving' regarding the prevention of Surgical Site Infections (SSI).
back:
* Showers: Reduce overall skin bacterial count using antiseptic soaps.
* Shaving: Increases infection risk via micro-abrasions; clipping hair is preferred if removal is necessary.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the primary physical method used to ensure that large-volume intravenous solutions are 'pyrogen-free' before being handled for invasive administration.
back:
* Filtration via 0.22 μm pore-size membranes.
* Physically traps bacteria, spores, and heat-resistant endotoxins.
* Prevents systemic inflammatory febrile reactions in the patient.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: The primary objective of sterilization, which utilizes autoclaving at 121°C, is the absolute destruction of all microbial life, specifically including highly resistant [___].
back:
Bacterial Spores.

*   Distinguishes sterilization from high-level disinfection.
*   Achieved via pressurized steam (121°C) or ethylene oxide gas.
*   Necessary for all surgical instruments (critical items).

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A hospitalized patient has a peripheral IV cannula in situ. On day 4, the site shows erythema and tenderness. Identify the immediate priority to prevent systemic sepsis.
back:
Prompt removal of the catheter.

*   Reduces source of local/systemic seeding.
*   Followed by site monitoring and clinical review.
*   Key principle: Removal of non-essential/infected invasive devices.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain the mechanical principle of 'Key-Part' protection within Aseptic Non-Touch Technique (ANTT).
back:
Strict non-contact with sterile components.

*   Key parts (e.g., syringe tips, needle hubs) must only touch other sterile parts.
*   Maintains a sterile pathway during device handling.
*   Protects critical sites (e.g., puncture site) from transient flora.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A surgical team prepares for a laparotomy while a ward doctor prepares to insert a peripheral IV. Contrast their required hand decontamination protocols.
back:
Surgical Scrub vs. Hand Hygiene.

*   Surgical: 2–6 minutes up to forearms; targets resident flora.
*   Standard Hygiene: Alcohol rub or handwash; targets transient flora.
*   Both mandatory before invasive procedures.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the preferred antiseptic agent and the specific application requirement before performing a central venous catheterization.
back:
2% Chlorhexidine in 70% Alcohol.

*   Must be allowed to dry completely via evaporation.
*   Provides superior residual antimicrobial activity over iodine.
*   Applied using a friction-based back-and-forth motion.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: According to WHO '5 Moments,' hand hygiene must be performed immediately [___] every aseptic procedure, regardless of glove use.
back:
Before.

*   Specifically Moment 2: Before a clean/aseptic procedure.
*   Protects the patient from microbes entering a sterile site.
*   Gloves do not replace the need for hand hygiene.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: To prevent Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection (CAUTI), describe the mandatory positioning of the drainage bag relative to the patient's anatomy.
back:
Always below the level of the bladder.

*   Prevents backflow (reflux) of contaminated urine.
*   Ensures continuous downhill drainage.
*   Drainage bag must never touch the floor.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Describe the mechanism by which indwelling invasive devices like CVCs or urinary catheters facilitate persistent iatrogenic infection.
back:
Formation of microbial Biofilms.

*   Microbes adhere to device surfaces and secrete a protective matrix.
*   Protects bacteria from antibiotics and host immune cells.
*   Mandates device removal to achieve clinical cure.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Contrast the clinical indication for using soap and water over alcohol-based hand rubs when handling invasive equipment in a gastroenterology ward.
back:
Visible soil or Spore exposure (e.g., C. difficile).

*   Alcohol does not kill spores or remove physical soil.
*   Mechanical friction of handwashing is required to rinse spores away.
*   Standard for diarrheal outbreaks.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: State the most effective daily clinical intervention for preventing Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP) and catheter-related infections.
back:
Daily review of device necessity.

*   Ensures prompt removal of redundant invasive devices.
*   Shortens the window of exposure to opportunistic pathogens.
*   Single best predictor of reduced infection rates.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: The vegetative cells of milk-borne pathogens such as Mycobacterium bovis and Brucella are traditionally eliminated using [___], which requires heating to 62°C for 30 minutes.
back:
- **Pasteurization**
- Kills vegetative cells but does not achieve sterilization
- Followed by rapid cooling to maintain liquid quality.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A 25-year-old male presents with deep second-degree burns. To prevent secondary wound infection, the clinician applies a specific heavy metal compound known as [___].
back:
- **Silver sulfadiazine**
- Silver binds to sulfhydryl groups to block enzymatic activity
- Bactericidal against a broad spectrum of burn pathogens.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain the immediate clinical protocol when a patient with an indwelling central venous catheter develops signs of local inflammation or purulent discharge.
back:
- **Immediate removal** of the suspected vascular device
- Culture the tip and insertion site
- Limit duration of future catheterization to prevent recurrence.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Contrast the evidence-based effectiveness of 'Surgical Technique' versus 'Fumigation' in the prevention of Surgical Site Infections (SSIs).
back:
- **Surgical technique**: Proven highly effective for SSI prevention
- **Fumigation**: Proven not effective; discarded in modern aseptic practice
- Focuses on clinical skill over environmental chemical sprays.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the quantitative measure used in microbiology to compare the antimicrobial efficacy of a chemical agent against a standardized concentration of phenol.
back:
- **Phenol Coefficient**
- A ratio of agent concentration to phenol concentration required for identical killing
- High values indicate superior potency over phenol.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: To effectively remove all bacteria and spores from heat-sensitive intravenous solutions, nitrocellulose filters must utilize a specific pore size of [___] μm.
back:
- **0.22 μm**
- Physically traps pathogens larger than the pore size
- Ensures solutions are pyrogen-free before clinical administration.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A clinician uses hypochlorite (bleach) to disinfect a blood spill. Describe the underlying biochemical mechanism by which this agent kills microorganisms.
back:
- **Oxidation**
- It cross-links essential sulfhydryl groups in microbial enzymes
- Forms inactive disulfide bonds, permanently inhibiting enzymatic activity.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the three specific items the nursing team must verbally confirm during the 'Before Skin Incision' phase of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist.
back:
- **Sterility confirmation** (including indicator results)
- Addressing equipment issues or concerns
- Confirmation that essential imaging is displayed.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Distinguish between the mechanisms of 'cationic detergents' (quaternary ammonium) and 'alcohols' regarding their interaction with bacterial cell membranes.
back:
- **Detergents**: Act as surfactants disrupting lipid membranes via hydrophobic chains
- **Alcohols**: Disorganize lipid structures and simultaneously denature proteins
- Both require water for maximal efficacy.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the practical clinical maneuver employed during invasive procedures to prevent contamination of sterile fields without requiring direct manual contact.
back:
- **No-touch technique**
- Prevents transfer of flora between staff and sterile sites
- Essential for safe handling of syringes and dressings.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: The chemical agent used for high-level disinfection of heat-sensitive invasive devices, such as endoscopes and respiratory therapy equipment, is [___].
back:
• Glutaraldehyde
• It is 10 times more effective than formaldehyde
• Used specifically for instruments that cannot tolerate autoclaving.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A patient with a central venous catheter (CVC) develops a fever and exit-site erythema. Explain the primary pathophysiological mechanism by which improper aseptic handling leads to catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSIs).
back:
• Formation of microbial biofilms on the catheter surface
• Migration of skin flora (e.g., S. epidermidis) along the external track
• Direct contamination of the catheter hub during access/manipulation.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which Chlorhexidine Gluconate provides superior persistent antimicrobial activity for surgical hand scrubbing compared to standard povidone-iodine.
back:
• Strong binding to the stratum corneum (skin proteins)
• Residual effect maintains low microbial counts for several hours
• Less affected by blood or organic matter compared to iodine.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Contrast the aseptic requirements of 'Surgical Asepsis' during an invasive laparotomy with 'Medical Asepsis' used in general ward procedures.
back:
• Surgical: Aim is complete elimination of all microorganisms/spores (sterile technique)
• Medical: Aim is reduction of number/transfer of pathogens (clean technique)
• Surgical requires sterile gowns/drapes; Medical relies on PPE and hand hygiene.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the mandatory pharmacological combination used for skin preparation prior to the insertion of high-risk invasive devices to achieve maximal rapid and persistent microbial kill.
back:
• 2% Chlorhexidine Gluconate in 70% Isopropyl Alcohol
• Alcohol provides immediate rapid kill
• Chlorhexidine provides long-term persistent antimicrobial protection.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: The standardized framework used to ensure that 'Key Parts' and 'Key Sites' of invasive devices remain uncontaminated during clinical procedures is known as the [___] technique.
back:
• ANTT (Aseptic Non-Touch Technique)
• Distinguishes between 'General' and 'Surgical' ANTT based on complexity
• Focuses on protecting aseptic fields and critical points of contact.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
coreConcept: WHO Five Moments and Device Handling
front: A clinician prepares to access a patient's IV line. Despite wearing clean gloves, identify the specific WHO 'Moment for Hand Hygiene' that must be performed to prevent iatrogenic infection.
back:
• Moment 2: Before a clean/aseptic procedure
• Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene
• Prevents the introduction of pathogens into the sterile bloodstream.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
coreConcept: Sharps Safety and Percutaneous Injury Prevention
front: Explain the microbiological risk associated with the 're-capping' of used needles and the subsequent handling of sharps in a clinical setting.
back:
• Primary cause of needle-stick injuries and percutaneous exposure
• Risk of transmitting blood-borne viruses (HBV, HCV, HIV)
• Mandates the use of 'sharps containers' and no-touch disposal.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Distinguish between the management of a 'Closed Drainage System' in urinary catheters versus an 'Open System' regarding infection risk.
back:
• Closed: Maintains a continuous sterile circuit to prevent ascending infection
• Open: High risk as it allows direct entry of bacteria into the bladder
• Closed systems are the gold standard for CAUTI prevention.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Name the specific physical barrier intervention utilized during the 'Time Out' phase of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist to ensure environmental sterility.
back:
• Sterile Draping
• Establishes a sterile field around the incision site
• Prevents transfer of microorganisms from non-sterile areas to the surgical wound.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: The standard parameters for moist heat sterilization in an autoclave require a temperature of 121°C at a pressure of [___] lb/in² for 15–20 minutes.
back: 15 lb/in²

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A post-operative patient has an indwelling urinary catheter. To minimize the risk of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection (CAUTI), the most critical maintenance principle regarding the drainage system is [___].
back: • Maintaining a strictly closed drainage system. • Ensuring the bag remains below bladder level. • Avoiding routine bladder irrigation.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain the chemical mechanism by which Ethylene Oxide (EO) gas achieves sterilization of heat-sensitive invasive surgical instruments.
back: • Alkylation of proteins and nucleic acids. • Substitutes hydroxyethyl groups for reactive hydrogen atoms. • Disrupts essential metabolic and reproductive processes of microorganisms.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Contrast the processing requirements for 'Critical' medical devices (e.g., surgical scalpels) versus 'Semi-critical' devices (e.g., flexible endoscopes) according to the Spaulding classification.
back: • Critical: Enters sterile tissue or vascular system; requires absolute sterilization. • Semi-critical: Contacts mucous membranes or non-intact skin; requires high-level disinfection (HLD).

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: State the clinical advantage of using Iodophors (iodine-detergent complexes) over Tincture of Iodine for invasive surgical skin preparation.
back: • Reduced skin irritation and toxicity. • Sustained release of free iodine for prolonged activity. • Solubility in water, making them easier to handle.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: To prevent Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP) in a patient with an invasive airway, the head-of-bed should be maintained at an angle of [___] degrees.
back: 30–45 degrees

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A surgical resident is inserting a central venous catheter. According to the 'Central Line Bundle,' list the necessary components of Maximal Sterile Barrier Precautions.
back: • Cap and mask. • Sterile gown and sterile gloves. • Large sterile drape covering the entire patient.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain the microbiological mechanism that necessitates the prompt removal of an invasive device (like a vascular catheter) when a device-related infection is suspected.
back: • Biofilm formation: Microbes produce a protective extracellular matrix. • Antibiotic resistance: The matrix prevents drug penetration. • Nidus of infection: Serves as a reservoir for persistent bacteremia.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Distinguish between 'Antisepsis' and 'Disinfection' in the context of clinical infection control.
back: • Antisepsis: Chemical killing of microbes on living tissue or skin surfaces. • Disinfection: Killing of many (but not all) microbes on inanimate objects/surfaces.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the primary antiseptic agents used for the 'surgical hand scrub' to achieve persistent antimicrobial activity before donning sterile gloves.
back: • Chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG). • Povidone-iodine (PVP-I). • Alcohol-based preparations with persistent biocidal activity.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
coreConcept: Principles of Aseptic Technique for Invasive Devices
front: The clinical protocol involving the use of sterile barriers and antiseptics during the insertion of invasive medical devices to prevent microbial entry is known as [___].
back: • Aseptic technique. • Employs sterile equipment, drapes, and skin preparation. • Critical for preventing device-associated infections such as CLABSIs and surgical site infections.

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: The specialized aseptic protocol involving sterile gowns, gloves, and full-body drapes used during the placement of a central line is known as [___].
back: • Full Barrier Precautions (Surgical Asepsis) • Protects the patient from skin and environmental microbes during invasive access • Significant measure in reducing Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI) incidence

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A patient's peripheral IV site appears erythematous with palpable cord-like veins and localized pain. Identify the immediate priority in the safe handling of this invasive device.
back: • Immediate removal of the device • Rotation of the insertion site to a different limb • Prevents progression to systemic bacteremia or suppurative thrombophlebitis

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain why the duration of an invasive device is considered the single most significant risk factor for healthcare-associated infections (HAIs).
back: • Provides a persistent portal of entry for pathogens • Allows for the development of protective biofilms on device surfaces • Increases the cumulative probability of aseptic technique breaches

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Contrast the aseptic technique requirements for 'Endotracheal Suctioning' versus 'Gastric Tube Aspiration'.
back: • Endotracheal: Requires surgical asepsis (sterile equipment) as the lower airway is sterile • Gastric: Requires medical asepsis (clean technique) as the stomach contains normal flora • Prevents ventilator-associated pneumonia

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Identify the primary evidence-based strategy for handling indwelling catheters to minimize the risk of bacterial colonization and infection.
back: • Daily assessment of device necessity • Early removal as soon as clinical indication ceases • Minimizes the window of opportunity for microbial entry and biofilm formation

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: In the prevention of catheter-related bloodstream infections, the [___] of the device must be scrubbed with an antiseptic for at least 15 seconds before any clinical access.
back: • Catheter Hub or Injection Port • Eliminates surface microbes before they are flushed into the circulation • Essential component of 'Aseptic Non-Touch Technique' (ANTT)

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: A medical student is observed recapping a hollow-bore needle after successfully obtaining an arterial blood gas sample. Identify the breach in safe handling and the correct procedural alternative.
back: • Breach: Manual recapping increases needle-stick injury and cross-contamination risk • Correct Action: Immediate disposal into a puncture-resistant sharps container at the point of use • Never bend or break needles

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Explain the 'Key-Part' and 'Key-Site' protection mechanism utilized in the Aseptic Non-Touch Technique (ANTT).
back: • Key-Parts (e.g., needle tips) and Key-Sites (e.g., insertion points) are critical entry points • These areas are contacted only by sterile equipment • Prevents cross-infection by guarding sterile-to-sterile contact

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: Distinguish between 'Surgical Asepsis' and 'Medical Asepsis' in the context of maintaining invasive devices.
back: • Surgical Asepsis: Elimination of all microorganisms (e.g., sterile field for device insertion) • Medical Asepsis: Reduction of pathogen count (e.g., hand hygiene and clean gloves for routine maintenance)

category: Explain aseptic technique and safe handling of invasive devices, in infection prevention
front: State the specific procedural rule regarding the physical level of a urinary drainage bag relative to the patient's bladder to ensure safe handling.
back: • Maintain bag below the level of the bladder at all times • Prevents retrograde reflux of stagnant, contaminated urine into the bladder • Bag must not touch the floor to avoid environmental contamination

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: To achieve complete sterilization of surgical instruments, an autoclave must reach a temperature of [___] at 15 lb/in² for at least 15 minutes.
back:
• 121°C (250°F)
• Required to kill highly resistant bacterial spores (e.g., Clostridium botulinum)
• Uses pressurized moist heat

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: A healthcare worker removes gloves after a dressing change and immediately prepares to examine the next patient. Explain the biological rationale for performing hand hygiene despite having worn gloves.
back:
• Gloves may have microscopic defects or tears
• Hands can become contaminated during the removal process
• Prevents transmission of flora acquired from the patient environment

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Explain the mechanical role of a "Closed Drainage System" in preventing catheter-associated infections in hospitalized patients.
back:
• Prevents entry of microorganisms into the bladder
• Eliminates the ascending route of infection through the lumen
• Reduces exposure to environmental contaminants

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: A clinician must prepare both the patient's skin and a surgical trolley. Contrast the safety profile and application of "Antiseptics" versus "Disinfectants" in this setting.
back:
• Antiseptics: Low toxicity; safe for living tissue/mucous membranes (e.g., ethanol)
• Disinfectants: High toxicity/corrosive; used only on inanimate objects (e.g., concentrated phenol)

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Identify the preferred sterilization method for heat-sensitive surgical materials, such as plastics, sutures, and specialized optical instruments.
back:
• Ethylene oxide gas (or X-ray radiation)
• Kills by alkylating proteins and nucleic acids
• Avoids structural damage caused by moist heat

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: The practice of using instruments rather than hands to handle sterile materials, or avoiding direct contact with used sharps, is defined as the [___].
back:
• "No-touch technique"
• Minimizes accidental transfer of microorganisms
• Core component of aseptic surgical practice

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: A nurse is disposing of a used syringe. According to standard safe work practices, specify the protocol for managing needles to prevent needle-stick injuries.
back:
• Never recap used needles
• Immediate disposal into puncture-proof "sharps" containers
• Use extreme care during handling and transfer

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Explain the clinical mechanism by which high-efficiency ventilation and "Dust Control" strategies reduce the risk of healthcare-associated infections.
back:
• Suppresses aerosolization of bacteria/viruses trapped in dust
• Removes droplet nuclei from the ambient air
• Prevents environmental contaminants from settling into sterile fields

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Distinguish between the microbial efficacy of "Pasteurization" and "Autoclaving" in the context of pathogen control.
back:
• Pasteurization: Kills vegetative pathogens (e.g., Salmonella); does not sterilize
• Autoclaving: Achieves total sterilization; kills all microbial life including spores

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Specify the primary chemical mechanism through which chlorine-based agents (e.g., hypochlorite) disinfect healthcare environments.
back:
• Powerful oxidizing agent
• Cross-links essential sulfhydryl groups in bacterial enzymes
• Forms inactive disulfide bonds, killing the microbe
